lead: Diffusion in a solid is the slow hopping of atoms between fixed sites, or the creep of gas molecules through tiny pores. The diffusivity D is far smaller than in a gas, often 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻²⁰ m²/s, and it rises steeply with temperature. Industry uses it to harden steel, dope silicon, dry wood and food, protect packaged food, and judge hydrogen loss from pipelines. Fick's laws still apply, but the concentration is inside the solid, and the surface value is fixed by solubility, not by the gas composition alone.
prereq: You need Fick's laws and the steady slab flux.

sections.h3: Mechanisms: how an atom gets past its neighbours

blocks.text: Textbooks split solid diffusion into two kinds. Structure-insensitive diffusion follows Fick's law through the solid itself, treated as a uniform material: a gas dissolving in and crossing a polymer film or a metal wall. Structure-sensitive diffusion runs through the pores and cracks of a porous solid such as a catalyst pellet, a dried clay or a bed of grain, so the pore geometry sets the rate.
In a metal or ceramic most atoms sit on lattice sites. Diffusion means an atom leaves one site and joins another. The path decides the speed.

items: Interstitial diffusion: small atoms such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen squeeze between host atoms. This is the fast path in steel treatment.
Vacancy or substitutional diffusion: an atom swaps places with an empty lattice site. This is slower and controls self-diffusion and alloy mixing.
Grain-boundary and surface diffusion: atoms along boundaries and free surfaces move faster than through the grain. These are fast paths in polycrystals, especially at low temperature.

Pore or Knudsen diffusion: a gas in a porous solid uses ordinary diffusion in large pores; in pores smaller than the mean free path, molecules hit walls more than each other. Porosity and tortuosity lower the effective D.

blocks.text: Fick's first law still holds: J<sub>A</sub> = −D dc<sub>A</sub>/dx. Here J<sub>A</sub> is the flux in mol/(m²·s), c<sub>A</sub> is concentration in mol/m³ of solid, x is position in m, and D is in m²/s. At the surface, equilibrium often gives c<sub>A</sub> = S p<sub>A</sub>, a Henry-type relation. Here p<sub>A</sub> is gas partial pressure in Pa and S is solubility in mol/(m³·Pa). So the gas composition alone does not set the surface concentration.

blocks.where: D is diffusivity (m²/s); D₀ is the pre-exponential factor (m²/s); E is activation energy (J/mol); R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); T is absolute temperature (K).

blocks.text: E is the energy barrier for one hop. Only the fraction exp(−E/RT) of atoms has enough thermal energy to cross it, so D climbs steeply as T rises. Near 700 K, a 100 K rise can multiply D by about 4 for the worked values below. Grain boundaries have a lower E than the lattice, so they dominate at low temperature. The figure plots D against T for D₀ = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and E = 60 kJ/mol; the marked points are the worked values.

sections.h3: Steady diffusion through a sheet, and where it is used

blocks.where: N<sub>A</sub> is steady flux (mol/(m²·s)); c<sub>A1</sub> and c<sub>A2</sub> are concentrations at the two faces (mol/m³); L is sheet thickness (m).

blocks.text: This is Fick's first law integrated across a flat sheet with constant flux. If one face touches a gas, use c<sub>A</sub> = S p<sub>A</sub>. Then N<sub>A</sub> = D S (p<sub>A1</sub> − p<sub>A2</sub>)/L, and the product D S is the permeability.

items: Carburizing and nitriding steel: carbon or nitrogen enters the hot surface and diffuses inward. Case depth grows with time; see unsteady-state diffusion.
Doping silicon wafers: phosphorus or boron is driven into silicon at high temperature to set electrical properties.
Drying wood, clay and food: moisture diffuses to the surface before evaporation. The drying chapters build drying-rate curves on this.
Polymer films in packaging: oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour permeate slowly through the film; low D keeps food fresh.
Hydrogen through pipeline steel: hydrogen is small and interstitial, so it can enter steel and cause embrittlement.
Membrane separation: differences in D and solubility separate gases or solutes; see membrane separations.

blocks.text: In a porous solid the gas diffuses through the pores, not the solid. Two corrections apply. The path is longer and narrower than the pellet, so D<sub>eff</sub> = ε D/τ, with porosity ε and tortuosity τ (often 2 to 6). When the pore radius r is smaller than the mean free path, molecules hit the walls more than each other, and the Knudsen diffusivity takes over: D<sub>K</sub> = 97 r (T/M)<sup>1/2</sup>, with D<sub>K</sub> in m²/s, r in m, T in K and M in kg/kmol. In between, the two resistances add: 1/D = 1/D<sub>AB</sub> + 1/D<sub>K</sub>.
Only a few syllabi add the Darken relation and the Kirkendall shift: two species with different D can interdiffuse, and inert markers move.

examples.question: For a gas in a metal take D₀ = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and E = 60 kJ/mol; R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). (a) Find D at 400 °C and at 500 °C. (b) A sheet 3 mm thick holds a steady concentration difference of 0.45 mol/m³ across it. Find the flux at 500 °C.
steps: Convert temperatures: 400 °C = 673 K and 500 °C = 773 K. Convert E: 60 kJ/mol = 60000 J/mol.
The ratio D(773 K)/D(673 K) = 1.76×10⁻⁹ / 4.41×10⁻¹⁰ = 4.0. A 100 K rise multiplies D by about 4.
examples.answer: D = 4.41×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 400 °C and 1.76×10⁻⁹ m²/s at 500 °C; the flux at 500 °C is 2.6×10⁻⁷ mol/(m²·s).

examples.question: A catalyst pellet has pores of mean radius 5.0 nm, porosity 0.40 and tortuosity 4.0. Nitrogen (M = 28 kg/kmol) diffuses in it at 500 K and 1 atm, where the molecular diffusivity of the gas pair is 5.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and the mean free path is about 0.11 µm. Find the effective diffusivity.
steps: Regime: the pore diameter, 10 nm, is about one-tenth of the 110 nm mean free path, so wall collisions dominate and Knudsen diffusion is expected.
Combine with molecular diffusion: 1/D = 1/(5.0×10⁻⁵) + 1/(2.05×10⁻⁶) = 2.0×10⁴ + 4.88×10⁵ = 5.08×10⁵ s/m², so D = 1.97×10⁻⁶ m²/s.
Pore geometry: D<sub>eff</sub> = ε D/τ = 0.40 × 1.97×10⁻⁶/4.0 = 1.97×10⁻⁷ m²/s.
examples.answer: D<sub>eff</sub> ≈ 2.0×10⁻⁷ m²/s, about 250 times smaller than the free-gas value. The Knudsen step alone cuts D by a factor of 25 and the pore geometry by another 10.

traps: Using a gas-phase diffusivity of order 10⁻⁵ m²/s for a solid. Solid D is often 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻²⁰ m²/s.
Putting E into RT in kJ/mol. Convert E to J/mol first; R is 8.314 J/(mol·K).
Setting the surface concentration from gas partial pressure alone. Use the Henry solubility c<sub>A</sub> = S p<sub>A</sub> for the solid.
Using lattice D when grain-boundary diffusion controls at low temperature, or using bulk D for a porous solid without porosity and tortuosity corrections.
Getting the sign wrong in Fick's law. Flux goes from high c to low c; c<sub>A1</sub> − c<sub>A2</sub> is positive when face 1 is richer.

quiz.q: In D = D₀ exp(−E/RT), what are D₀ and E, with units?
quiz.a: D₀ is the pre-exponential factor in m²/s; E is the activation energy in J/mol.

quiz.q: Why is D in a solid much smaller than in a gas, and why does it rise steeply with temperature?
quiz.a: Atoms in a solid are held near fixed sites, so movement needs a site change or a pore path. Only a small fraction exp(−E/RT) has enough energy to cross the barrier, so D rises steeply with T.

quiz.q: A sheet 2 mm thick has D = 5.0×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s and a steady concentration difference of 0.30 mol/m³. Find the flux.
A polycrystalline metal shows faster diffusion at low temperature than a single crystal of the same metal. Explain.
quiz.a: Grain boundaries are disordered fast paths with lower activation energy than the lattice. At low T the lattice hop rate is very small, so grain-boundary diffusion dominates.

quiz.q: Why does a gas partial pressure not directly give the surface concentration in a solid?
quiz.a: The solid dissolves only part of the gas. Equilibrium is Henry-type, c<sub>A</sub> = S p<sub>A</sub>, so solubility S is also needed.

quiz.q: Low diffusivity helps in a food-packaging film but is not enough in a hydrogen pipeline. Explain both.
quiz.a: In packaging, a low D times a low solubility (a low permeability D S) slows oxygen and water vapour entry, so food stays fresh. Hydrogen is a small interstitial atom, so even near room temperature its D in steel is not negligible: it enters, collects at defects and causes embrittlement. The same law N = D S Δp/L governs both; what differs is the size of D S for the species involved.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern work measures solid diffusion with atom-probe tomography and secondary-ion mass spectrometry, and predicts hop barriers with density-functional theory. Hydrogen embrittlement of pipeline steels is an active area because small interstitial H moves even near room temperature. Polymer films show concentration-dependent D, so simple Fick plots bend. Search next for interstitial diffusion, Knudsen diffusion, carburizing, and hydrogen permeation.
